chunks.content: 1 INTRODUCTION Generating and translating high‐quality evidence is integral to providing safe and effective medication management for residents of aged care homes. Despite this, residents of aged care homes are often under‐represented in research, with only 2% of studies involving older people being conducted in the aged care home setting, resulting in evidence gaps. , These gaps present a challenge to clinicians because evidence from clinical trials and observational studies on community‐dwelling older adults cannot necessarily be extrapolated to residents of aged care homes. Residents of aged care homes are often older and frailer with higher rates of cognitive impairment and polypharmacy. This means that residents may be particularly vulnerable to adverse drug events and have different treatment benefits and risks than robust community‐dwelling older adults. , These factors may necessitate different strategies for evidence generation and translation. Evidence translation can depend on the nature of evidence generation, and vice versa. Considering barriers and facilitators to evidence translation when designing research can help facilitate the uptake and sustainability of evidence‐based interventions. , , Previous systematic reviews report challenges of conducting research and translating evidence in aged care homes. , , A recent scoping review found tailored education and peer champions are successful for implementing interventions. Knowledge brokers can act as peer champions to implement tailored strategies for knowledge translation. , To our knowledge, no reviews have explored generating and translating evidence in the aged care setting. Existing reviews have been conducted in acute care, outpatient and primary care settings, which are not specific to aged care homes. , Medication management in this narrative review refers to the prescribing, dispensing, administration and monitoring of medications. It consists of activities and processes that ensure the safe and effective use of medications at each episode of care. This narrative review will explore opportunities and challenges for generating and translating evidence for safe and effective medication management in aged care homes with key examples related to prevalent and high‐risk medications. A non‐systematic search of bibliometric databases including PubMed, Embase and Google Scholar was conducted across the domains of aged care homes (e.g. ‘nursing home’, ‘long‐term care’, ‘residential aged care’, ‘aged care home’), medications (e.g. ‘medication’, ‘medicine’, ‘medication management’), and evidence generation and translation (e.g. ‘barrier’, ‘facilitator’, ‘randomised control trial’, ‘cohort study’, ‘implementation’, ‘knowledge translation’). Key articles that addressed generating and translating evidence in aged care were included. Reference lists of relevant studies were also reviewed to identify key articles for inclusion. 1.1 Need for evidence in relation to outcomes prioritized by residents, carers and aged care provider organizations Few studies assess non‐pharmacological outcomes integral to the holistic care of residents of aged care homes. These include outcomes such as emotions, mood, or the impact on social life that are prioritized by people living with Alzheimer's disease. The Lancet Commission on Long Term‐Care for Older Persons has recognized the need for better integration of medical and social services to allow residents to remain engaged in meaningful and fulfilling activities. Nearly two‐thirds of participants in the World Health Organization (WHO) Research Priorities to Reduce the Global Burden of Dementia initiative prioritized the need for better study outcome measures. Residents of aged care homes may have different goals of care when compared to robust community‐dwelling older adults. For example, residents with limited life expectancy may prioritize symptom management rather than long‐term prevention. Older adults living with dementia may prioritize outcomes such as quality of life, pill burden, falls risk and avoidance of hospitalizations when deciding whether or not to take antihypertensive medications. A systematic review reported patient involvement in developing core outcome sets increased the likelihood of including quality of life outcomes. Involving residents and carers in selecting research outcomes may help overcome the gaps between common clinical trial outcomes and those prioritized by residents. Including residents and informal carers in Guideline Development Groups may be important because residents may have different treatment preferences to clinicians or care home staff. The Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation (GRADE) evidence‐to‐decision framework provides a mechanism to consider resident and carer perspectives when developing clinical practice guidelines. Despite this, resident involvement in evidence‐synthesis and clinical decision‐making remains limited, although there is some evidence that this is changing. A study involving aged care home staff and resident co‐design of an aged care home service to improve resident wellbeing highlighted the value of resident involvement, reporting strengthened resident‐staff relationships, resident reported satisfaction and improved staff capacity to advocate for resident needs and values. The Clinical Practice Guidelines and Principles of Care for People with Dementia were developed with carer and aged care provider organization input to help ensure recommendations were relevant to the needs of end‐users of the Guidelines. 1.2 Need for clinical decision support in relation to medication prescribing in aged care homes Prescribing decisions in the aged care home

The Clinical Practice Guidelines and Principles of Care for People with Dementia were developed with carer and aged care provider organization input to help ensure recommendations were relevant to the needs of end‐users of the Guidelines. 1.2 Need for clinical decision support in relation to medication prescribing in aged care homes Prescribing decisions in the aged care home setting can be challenging due to apparent evidence inconsistencies. The SPRINT trial reported intensive blood pressure lowering to <120 mmHg reduced the risk of cardiovascular events and mortality compared to blood pressure <140 mmHg in participants aged ≥75 years. While SPRINT is often used to justify antihypertensive prescribing for older people, SPRINT excluded people living in aged care homes and those living with dementia. In contrast, the PARTAGE study demonstrated combination antihypertensive therapy in residents of aged care homes with blood pressure <130 mmHg was associated with a higher risk of mortality. Another example of clinical uncertainty relates to prescribing bisphosphonates for osteoporosis. Qualitative research suggests clinicians are uncertain about prescribing and deprescribing for people with dementia, limited mobility and in the context of limited bone densitometry undertaken in the aged care home setting. Most international osteoporosis guidelines ( n = 29, 69%) refer to deprescribing of bisphosphonates in the context of drug holidays, which are not advised for patients at high‐risk of fractures and most of these guidelines do not make specific deprescribing recommendations for residents with limited life expectancy. High‐risk medications including warfarin, insulins, oral antiplatelet agents and oral hypoglycaemic agents are not generally classified as potentially inappropriate medications (PIMs) but are implicated in two‐thirds of all adverse drug event related emergency department presentations of older adults in the United States (US). Glucose‐lowering medications are important for achieving glycaemic control but 5–86% of residents are potentially over‐treated and 1–35% potentially under‐treated for diabetes in aged care homes, suggesting a high degree of variability in pharmacological management of diabetes. This highlights the importance of healthcare professionals and care staff being aware of these high‐risk medications, in addition to PIMs, and the importance of ensuring both resident and system‐level processes are in place to minimize the risk of errors and medication‐related harm. Lack of aged care specific evidence‐based guidelines has been described as a barrier to deprescribing. Process evaluations of deprescribing interventions help generate evidence on contextual factors integral to deprescribing. , Development of deprescribing guidelines could be aided by international deprescribing networks such as those established in Canada, Australia, US and Europe and national deprescribing policies. , Medication‐related clinical decision support tools synthesize evidence‐based recommendations to inform medication prescribing decisions, usually at the point of care. Many clinical decision support tools and explicit criteria for PIMs, such as Beers Criteria and the Screening Tool of Older Persons' Prescriptions (STOPP) and Screening Tool to Alert to Right Treatment (START) criteria are not specific to the aged care home or end‐of‐life care settings. Despite being originally proposed for residents in aged care homes, Beers Criteria are now intended for all adults aged 65 years and older except in hospice and end‐of‐life care settings. A study conducted in the US highlighted the need for consensus recommendations for appropriate prescribing in residents living with advanced dementia, to decrease polypharmacy and minimize the use of medications that are high‐risk or of minimal benefit. Identifying residents most at‐risk of preventable medication‐related harm in aged care homes is complicated because the implicated medications are not necessarily inappropriate for all residents. A range of multidisciplinary staff are involved in medication management. For example, care staff spend considerable time with residents and have an important influence on medication decision‐making. Engaging all stakeholders in medication management interventions may facilitate antipsychotic deprescribing in residents living with dementia. A qualitative study involving United Kingdom (UK) aged care homes reported modifications were required to make deprescribing tools suitable for the aged care setting. Developing clinical decision support tools for aged care staff may empower aged care staff to advocate for residents and support shared decision‐making. 2 GENERATING EVIDENCE Despite under‐representation of residents in pivotal randomized controlled trials (RCTs), there is an increasing number of clinical trials and observational studies conducted in the aged care home setting. A systematic mapping review of RCTs reported that there were at least 292 RCTs conducted in aged care homes internationally between 1974 and 2009, with half of these studies published between 2003 and 2009. These studies focused on behaviour, prescribing and malnutrition. A systematic mapping review of RCTs reported that there were at least 292 RCTs conducted in aged care homes internationally between 1974 and 2009, with half of these studies published between 2003 and 2009. These studies focused on behaviour, prescribing and malnutrition. Of 397 intervention studies in aged care homes from 2015 to 2022, the most common intervention related to medication management ( n = 56, 14.1%). It is unclear if the number of studies conducted in the aged care home setting has continued to increase in recent years. 2.1 RCTs RCTs are regarded as the gold standard study design for evaluating medication efficacy and safety. This is because randomization minimizes bias by balancing known and unknown confounding factors across study groups. Despite residents of aged care homes being among the most vulnerable population groups, and the first to be vaccinated in many countries, <10% of participants in COVID‐19 vaccine clinical trials were aged 65 years or older and <1% were 85 years or older. Of 39 RCTs conducted in Australian aged care homes from 2000 to 2018, the most common focus areas were dementia, falls prevention and mental health. Most RCTs were not focused on medication efficacy or safety and few assessed resident quality of life as recommended by the Lancet Commission on Long Term‐Care for Older Persons. , Traditional RCTs often have a rigid study design that can be challenging to implement for investigating medication management interventions in an aged care home setting. This is because routines may be inflexible, staff may have competing clinical care priorities between residents, and residents may experience fluctuations in cognitive function and behaviours. Investigators will need to consider these factors when obtaining consent, undertaking data collection and resident follow‐up. RCTs that measure outcomes prioritized by residents may not provide evidence on hard endpoints typically measured in RCTs. However, novel trial designs such as stepped‐wedge and helix counterbalanced designs have been used to overcome the limitations of traditional RCTs such as small sample sizes, need to adjust for aged care home characteristics and participant drop‐out following randomization into the control rather than intervention group. , , 2.2 Conducting observational studies High‐quality observational studies can also help address the evidence‐gap arising from under‐representation of residents of aged care homes in RCTs. Cohort and case–control study designs permit analyses for large and generalizable resident samples. For example, a large cohort study based on a US Medicare aged care home sample with 2‐year follow up reported similar rates of injurious falls and cardiovascular events following commencement of a first‐line antihypertensive in residents with limited life expectancy. Observational studies also allow for investigation of important outcomes that may not occur in the context of RCTs that have small sample sizes and short durations. For example, a nested case–control study involving aged care home residents found that current use of antipsychotic medications appeared to be associated with a slightly increased risk of hip fracture compared to nonusers (adjusted odds ratio = 1.26, 95% confidence interval [CI] = 1.05–1.52). Cohort and case–control studies are also relatively low cost compared to RCTs. Methods such as propensity score matching and inverse probability of treatment weighting can be used in these studies to account for possible bias and confounding. However, prevalent‐user designs that involve cross‐sectional medication exposure assessment may be particularly problematic for analytical studies in the aged care home setting because clinicians may selectively deprescribe medications for the frailest subset of residents who are at highest risk of adverse events, hospitalization or death. This means that nonusers of the medication under investigation may comprise both never‐users and those who discontinued (e.g. due to lack of efficacy, adverse events or change of treatment goals). Although new‐user designs overcome some of the limitations of prevalent‐user designs, new‐user designs are challenging to implement in the aged care home setting as residents are often long‐term users of the medication under investigation prior to entry into the aged care home. Drug utilization studies are important for identifying areas for quality improvement initiatives. For example, a 2024 repeated cross‐sectional study reported an increase in antidepressant use among residents of aged care homes. Understanding the strengths and limitations of different data sources is particularly relevant to the aged care home setting because medications are often charted for regular or as‐needed administration, may be medical or nurse‐initiated, or be unable to be consumed as intended (e.g. due to swallowing difficulties). When interpreting medication prevalence estimates from drug use studies, clinicians and policymakers should consider the data source and exposure time window. When interpreting medication prevalence estimates from drug use studies, clinicians and policymakers should consider the data source and exposure time window. For example, a systematic review of opioid use in Australian aged care homes reported 28–34% of residents were prescribed regular opioids over windows of 1 week to 1 month but 27–50% of residents were dispensed opioids over a 12‐month window. The Neurological and Mental Health Global Epidemiology Network (NeuroGEN) is an international big‐data platform used to facilitate high‐quality observational studies. NeuroGEN comprises 15 databases with data for >320 million individuals. International multidatabase pharmacoepidemiological research using common study protocols and common data models can improve generalizability of research findings. 2.3 Barriers and facilitators to generating evidence in the aged care home setting Research in the aged care home setting considers resident‐, facility‐ and system‐level factors that may influence the uptake, conduct and success of the research (Figure ). , , , , , These factors may be specific to aged care home, and therefore researchers need to invest time into understanding each local context. Reported rates of resident recruitment for prospective studies have ranged from 0–42%. Obtaining ethical written informed consent from residents, particularly those with cognitive impairment or their carers, can be resource intensive and require multiple conversations at different times or days to accommodate resident and carer schedules or health status. , Successful recruitment typically involves allocating appropriate written and staffing‐related resources for these conversations, including staff attending in‐person and the development of concise, lay‐language study materials. Not allocating adequate resources for resident recruitment could lead to under‐representation of residents with dementia who may not be able to provide written informed consent themselves. Also, recruitment may be maximized by providing information for residents, carers and aged care home staff in different formats, for example, information sessions, posters and videos. , In the SIMPLER trial, written information for residents and carers was prepared in accordance with the Dementia Australia Guide to Dementia Friendly Language, and the study nurses who recruited residents were trained in Dementia Australia Let us talk tips. Cognitive screening tools such as the Evaluation to Sign Consent measure and Brief Interview for Mental Status (BIMS) can be used to initially screen resident ability to consent to participate in research. Evaluation to Sign Consent has demonstrated some evidence of reliability and validity. An observational study compared BIMS scores with aged care home staff assessments of resident capacity and found that the higher the BIMS score (indicating greater intact cognition), the more likely the aged care home staff were to assess the resident as being able to consent ( P < .001). Although cognitive screening tools may support initial screening for recruitment, they should not substitute rigorous assessment of a resident's ability to provide full consent. In addition to supporting resident involvement in research, establishing effective and genuine partnerships with aged care organizations and aged care home staff is critical for success. Engaging aged care providers as research partners in the conceptualization and design phase can help ensure that the research addresses shared priorities, and that appropriate and acceptable structures and processes are put in place to address potential industry‐wide barriers such as workloads, staff turnover and staff knowledge on the importance of research. While providing clinical care is the highest priority for aged care organizations, research has an important role in improving the quality and efficiency of care. High‐quality clinical care and research are not mutually exclusive and delivering high‐quality clinical care is dependent on access to robust evidence. It is possible that different aged care organizations place a different level of emphasis on research and therefore the results of research conducted with one organization may not necessarily be generalizable to the wider aged care sector. Increasing use of electronic point‐of‐care systems and linked data may also facilitate more timely and granular data access, and may help to reduce the burden of data collection. 3 TRANSLATING EVIDENCE Efficient and timely translation of evidence into practice can support the delivery of high‐quality, evidence‐based care. Poor uptake of evidence and clinical practice guidelines is a known barrier to high‐quality care across all health settings, yet research into strategies specific to the aged care home setting is lacking, particularly in relation to improving medication management. A 2022 overview of systematic reviews of strategies for implementing clinical practice guidelines found only 4 (11%) studies were conducted in the aged care home setting. 3.1 Strategies for facilitating

Poor uptake of evidence and clinical practice guidelines is a known barrier to high‐quality care across all health settings, yet research into strategies specific to the aged care home setting is lacking, particularly in relation to improving medication management. A 2022 overview of systematic reviews of strategies for implementing clinical practice guidelines found only 4 (11%) studies were conducted in the aged care home setting. 3.1 Strategies for facilitating evidence translation Effective translation helps to ensure delivery of consistent, evidence‐based care. Several strategies can be implemented to facilitate evidence translation in aged care homes (Figure ). , , , , Sustained implementation of guideline recommendations is challenging, with current literature reporting only one‐third of guideline recommendations are sustained over‐time. Evidence translation strategies can be guided by a knowledge translation or implementation framework such as the Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research (CFIR) , and Integrated Promoting Action on Research Implementation in Health Services (i‐PARIHS) framework. Application of these frameworks requires a sound understanding of aged care management structures governance, local policy and procedures and staff and resident characteristics. A process evaluation study of a cluster RCT performed in Dutch aged care homes applied CFIR and found that peer champions aided the implementation of an electronic health record tool for empirical treatment of urinary tract infections. Local factors such as time constraints, staffing levels and access to resources have been identified as common barriers to clinical practice guideline implementation in the aged care home setting. These barriers may be addressed through achieving leadership buy‐in and ensuring adequate financial resources for implementation. Adequate staffing with an appropriate skill‐mix to accommodate research tasks should be accounted for in the research budget. 3.1.1 Audit and feedback Audit and feedback is a widely used strategy for implementation of new evidence into clinical practice. Audit and feedback reviews current clinical practice against explicit standards and uses this data to develop, implement and evaluate quality improvement initiatives. A Cochrane review assessed the effects of audit and feedback on professional practice and healthcare outcomes and reported a median 4.3% (interquartile range 0.5–16%) absolute improvement in healthcare professional adherence to the desired standard of practice. Repeating audit and feedback cycles has the potential to generate a cumulative incremental improvement to professional practice or healthcare outcomes. An audit and feedback intervention addressing high‐risk prescriptions in Canadian aged care homes reported a good return of investment of 1.02 (95% CI 0.51–1.93) for every C$1 spent on the intervention. Furthermore, effective provision of context‐specific feedback is important for practice change. This may include repeat feedback in both written and verbal format with explicit targets and an action plan. 3.1.2 Quality indicators Quality indicators are one method of auditing clinical care in aged care homes. Mandatory reporting of aged care home quality indicators has been in place in the US since 2002 and more recently was implemented in Australia in 2019. , Guidelines such as the 2021 Society for Post‐Acute and Long‐Term Care Medicine Pain Management Guideline and 2019 Infectious Diseases Society of America Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management of Asymptomatic Bacteriuria are being published with quality indicators that can be used by aged care homes and healthcare professionals to audit concordance with best practice. , While these indicators can be useful for auditing, the governance structures supporting a feedback loop to inform iterative practice change is often missing or is reliant on proactive individuals. 3.1.3 Local action plans Local action plans can be informed by audits and quality indicator data. A pragmatic RCT in Canadian aged care homes demonstrated that feedback approaches involving goal setting and written action plans were effective in improving care aide involvement in communication about resident care. Furthermore, developing and implementing local action plans through a dementia care quality improvement collaborative increased community, hospital and aged care clinician self‐reported guideline adherence by 41.2% ( P = .012, CI 1.08–1.87). Clinicians applied the plan‐do‐study‐act model to develop their own implementation plan to generate iterative improvements in guideline adherence. Local action plans created by individuals or collaboratives with a comprehensive understanding of the local context may have the potential to improve guideline adherence, particularly if used in conjunction with other knowledge translation strategies such as audit and feedback. 3.1.4 Education and training Education and training builds the capacity of staff to address existing knowledge gaps but requires organizational support to encourage and reinforce learning and provide additional paid work time. Academic detailing is a form of education outreach that involves synthesizing evidence into a simplified format and presenting this to a clinician via interactive discussion. Academic detailing is a form of education outreach that involves synthesizing evidence into a simplified format and presenting this to a clinician via interactive discussion. A Cochrane review of education outreach on professional practice and healthcare outcomes reported a 5.6% (interquartile range 3.0–9.0%) median adjusted risk difference in compliance with desired practice. The adjusted risk differences for prescribing were highly consistent, but were variable for other types of professional activities. An antimicrobial stewardship programme, which delivered education and training to aged care home clinicians on antimicrobial prescribing and the use of antimicrobial stewardship tools reported a significant 16% reduction in resistance to fluoroquinolone antibiotic ofloxacin ( P = .004). Clinician unfamiliarity with clinical practice guidelines or preference to use own pre‐existing knowledge has been highlighted as a common barrier to uptake. , , Provision of education and training to aged care home staff can promote awareness, interpretation and application of guidelines. Companion resources such as point of care checklists to support clinical decision making and concise guideline summaries may facilitate guideline awareness, familiarity and adherence. There may be benefit in producing consumer resources in different languages to support evidence uptake in culturally and linguistically diverse communities within the same country. For example, Australia's new companion guide accompanying The Clinical Practice Guidelines for the Appropriate Use of Psychotropic Medications in People Living with Dementia and in Residential Aged Care has been translated into simplified and traditional Mandarin, Vietnamese, Greek and Italian. 3.2 Knowledge brokers to facilitate knowledge translation Knowledge brokers are individuals or groups who act as intermediaries to move knowledge from those who produce it (e.g. guideline developers) to those that use it (e.g. clinicians). They act as knowledge managers, linkage agents and capacity builders. Knowledge brokers have been primarily used in the hospital setting to facilitate guideline implementation, but are increasingly being used in the aged care home setting. , They may use a variety of knowledge translation strategies, including education, local action plans, development of guideline implementation tools, and audit and feedback, to build the capacity and capability of staff and systems to implement new guidelines. Knowledge brokers have been shown to improve guideline adherence in up to 63% of studies, but there is a paucity of evidence on their effectiveness and cost‐effectiveness in the aged care home setting. 4 FUTURE DIRECTIONS 4.1 International knowledge sharing There is increasing recognition of the value of international research collaboration. This has been highlighted by the United Nations and WHO through the 2021–2030 Decade of Healthy Aging. In 2021, WHO launched the Global Dementia Observatory Knowledge Exchange Platform. Through this initiative, resources submitted to the Platform are peer‐reviewed and mapped to strategic action areas of the Global Action Plan on the Public Health Response to Dementia 2017–2025. Other initiatives to share knowledge between countries include the Guidelines International Network library and registry of guidelines in development. Specific research networks, such as the UK National Institute for Health and Care Research—Enabling Research in Care Homes (ENRICH) programme, enable knowledge sharing to help to identify areas of best practice and opportunities for improvement. Understanding the value of specific evidence for informing policy and practice is often dependent on appreciating similarities and differences in aged care systems across states and countries. A recent study that investigated transferability of aged care research between 7 countries (Australia, Canada, Japan, New Zealand, Switzerland, UK and USA) reported that these countries were superficially comparable in terms of the percentage gross domestic product spent on aged care homes and proportion of residents living with dementia. However, the lack of standardization on how aged care home data are reported compromises opportunities for international comparisons. Core outcome sets developed with resident and carer input may provide opportunities to measure outcomes that are prioritized by residents and support national and international comparisons across different studies. 4.2 Optimizing use of technology Digitalization and increasing access to routinely collected administrative health data (e.g. pharmacy claims and hospital records) are creating new opportunities for conducting cohort and case control studies in aged care homes. The Long‐Term Care Data Cooperative funded by the National Institute on Aging links resident electronic health records with Medicare claims in the USA. In August 2022, this cooperative included 1000 aged care homes with the aim to increase access to timely clinical data for research. Data linkage may provide new opportunities for analysing outcomes prioritized by residents and carers, for example, cognition, physical function and behaviours. and increasing access to routinely collected administrative health data (e.g. pharmacy claims and hospital records) are creating new opportunities for conducting cohort and case control studies in aged care homes. The Long‐Term Care Data Cooperative funded by the National Institute on Aging links resident electronic health records with Medicare claims in the USA. In August 2022, this cooperative included 1000 aged care homes with the aim to increase access to timely clinical data for research. Data linkage may provide new opportunities for analysing outcomes prioritized by residents and carers, for example, cognition, physical function and behaviours. New information technology infrastructure that enables the use of real‐time data analytics may support clinical decision‐making. Real‐time predictive analytic dashboards embedded into aged care homes have been developed, allowing for timely integration of resident health information. Web‐based tools such as The Goal‐directed Medication review Electronic Decision Support System (G‐MEDSS) is an example of a digital clinical decision support system tool that addresses the need for resident medication goals of care to be integrated into clinical reviews. 5 CONCLUSION Developing and strengthening strategies for generating and translating evidence in the aged care home setting is imperative to bridge existing evidence gaps for safe and effective medication management and improved resident outcomes. Facilitators of evidence generation and translation into the aged care home setting could guide opportunities to facilitate robust research. These facilitators include effective partnerships with aged care homes, establishing research networks and embedded knowledge brokers. Integrating outcomes prioritized by residents and aged care organizations into future research and resident involvement in evidence‐synthesis can ensure medication management strategies developed are tailored to residents' needs, supporting improved quality of life and preventing medication‐related harms. Introduction Postoperative delirium (POD), which is an acute and transitory brain condition, includes focus problems, disruptions in consciousness, and notable oscillations in cognitive function. POD is defined as delirium that manifests within a week following surgery and mainly occurs within 24–72 hours [ ] . HIGHLIGHTS There was just one type of patient in this trial, and there were very few intervening variables that could have affected the result. Although POD typically occurs in the first 72 hours after surgery, we followed up patients to discharge or postoperative day 5 to evaluate the entire postoperative period in which delirium is diagnosed. We had a high rate of in-person delirium assessment completion, which is challenging, with a rigorous protocol evaluating for delirium twice daily to capture the waxing and waning nature of the disorder. The number of elderly people undergoing arthroscopy and joint replacement surgeries in China is increasing as the population ages. However, POD is one of the most prevalent postoperative complications after orthopedic joint replacement surgery, occurring in 4–54.3% of elderly people after joint replacement surgery [ , ] . In addition to extending hospital stays, increasing costs, and necessitating specialized care after discharge, POD also increases the risk of complications such as pressure ulcers, dementia, pulmonary infections, urinary incontinence, and impaired joint function recovery immediately after surgery. It even increases the risk of death [ – ] . Thus, medical professionals must be diligent in preventing POD. Delirium has a complicated and multifaceted etiology [ , ] . Current research indicates that POD may be related to the mitochondrial dysfunction caused by anesthesia or surgery [ – ] . It has also been suggested that the restoration of mitochondrial activity can relieve postoperative cognitive impairment [ – ] . Considering that delirium and cognitive impairment are related and share common triggers, we speculate that focusing on mitochondria could be a potential way to prevent older patients from developing POD. The application of methylene blue (MB) in some surgical procedures has been considered safe. Studies have shown that MB can improve brain metabolism and restore mitochondrial function as a redox mediator in the electron transfer chain [ , ] . Moreover, MB can swiftly penetrate the blood‒brain barrier, infiltrate cerebral tissue, and accumulate in the mitochondria and cytoplasm of neurons [ ] . So we hypothesize that infusion of 2 mg/kg of MB within 60 minutes after induction of anesthesia can effectively reduce the incidence of POD (assessed using the Confusion Assessment Method scale) in elderly joint replacement patients without increasing the incidence of perioperative adverse events (AEs). Therefore, we designed this randomized controlled clinical trial to investigate whether MB can reduce the incidence of POD in elderly patients undergoing joint replacement surgery. Materials and methods This single-blind randomized and controlled trial followed the CONSORT criteria [ ] and the TITAN Guidelines [ ] . This clinical study was approved by the Ethics Committee of the hospital on 3 July 2023 and registered at the China Clinical Trial Center on 27 July 2023. After providing the participants with oral and written information about the study, written informed consent was obtained from the patients or a member of their immediate family. Patients recruitment All elderly patients scheduled to undergo joint replacement surgery in the surgical unit underwent preoperative screening with the Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE) and Confusion Assessment Method (CAM) scales. The inclusion criteria were as follows: (1) underwent elective joint replacement surgery under general anesthesia; (2) were aged ≥ 65 years; and (3) were willing to complete the neuropsychological assessment and were accessible for in-person follow-up interviews. The exclusion criteria were as follows: (1) preoperative dementia, severe depression, or severe psychological or neurological conditions; (2) allergy to 6-phospho-glucose dehydrogenase absence (favism) or hypersensitivity to MB; (3) drug or alcohol abuse or taking medications that may result in drug reactions, such as selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors or serotonin and norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors; (4) prior major brain injury; (5) emergency surgery; (6) serious medical conditions (such as severe liver or renal dysfunction, severe pulmonary hypertension, heart failure, and respiratory failure); (7) inability to complete scale assessments (such as significant sight, hearing, or linguistic impairments); (8) participation in other experimental studies within 3 months; and (9) preoperative MMSE score: illiterate MMSE < 17 points; primary school (≤6 years of education): MMSE < 20 points; and secondary school or above (>6 years of education): MMSE < 24 points. The withdrawal criteria were as follows: (1) severe AEs such as massive bleeding or intraoperative rescue and (2) admission to the intensive care unit (ICU) after surgery. 3 months; and (9) preoperative MMSE score: illiterate MMSE < 17 points; primary school (≤6 years of education): MMSE < 20 points; and secondary school or above (>6 years of education): MMSE < 24 points. The withdrawal criteria were as follows: (1) severe AEs such as massive bleeding or intraoperative rescue and (2) admission to the intensive care unit (ICU) after surgery. Randomization and blinding The eligible individuals were assigned to the MB group or the control group (1:1). A researcher used basic randomization with numbers produced by SPSS software. Each sequentially numbered envelope contained the grouping, which was stored in an opaque and sealed envelope. When the participants entered the surgical area, the anesthesiologist opened the envelope and administered the intervention as planned appropriately, so the anesthesiologist was not blinded to the grouping. Patients were not blinded to the grouping, which may be predicted by the blue color of the urine. The urine bags of each individual were wrapped in a black plastic bag after surgery, and the patient’s family members were told not to inform the patients and postoperative follow-up staff of the color of urine until the urine tubes were removed. As a result, this clinical investigation was single-blind, randomized, and controlled. Intervention measures and perioperative management Within 60 minutes of anesthesia induction, the MB group received a continuous intravenous infusion of 50 mL of a mixture of 2 mg/kg of MB and 5% glucose solution, while the control group received the same quantity of 5% glucose solution continuously. The venous access was opened, and noninvasive blood pressure, ECG, pulse oxygen saturation, and invasive arterial blood pressure were monitored once the patient entered the room. Sufentanil (0.3–0.6 mg/kg), rocuronium (0.6 mg/kg), and etomidate (0.3 mg/kg) were used to induce general anesthesia. An endotracheal tube or laryngeal mask was inserted after the patient’s consciousness disappeared and the muscle relaxed. Propofol 4–6 mg/(kg ·h) and remifentanil 0.1–0.3 mg/(kg ·min) were intravenously infused, and 1% sevoflurane was continuously inhaled to maintain Bispectral Index (BIS) values between 40 and 60. After the patients were given general anesthetics, the following procedures were performed: for individuals who had knee replacements, a routine femoral nerve block was performed; and for patients who had hip replacements, a femoral nerve block + lateral femoral cutaneous nerve block was performed. To maintain stable perioperative hemodynamics, vasoactive medications such as atropine, ephedrine, and phenylephrine hydrochloride were used when needed. Maintaining the intraoperative blood pressure at ±20% of the baseline mean arterial pressure is recommended. The addition of muscle relaxants depended on the intraoperative circumstances. Record the person’s use of the “cocktail” therapy and patient-controlled intravenous analgesia. Patient-controlled intravenous analgesia with 2 mg/kg sufentanil, 6 mg tropisetron, and saline to 100 mL was applied for postoperative analgesia. The continuous infusion rate of the patient-controlled pump was set at 2 mL/h, the self-controlled analgesic dose was 0.5 mL, and the occlusion interval was 15 minutes. Muscle relaxants and inhalation anesthetics were stopped 30 minutes before the end of the operation. At the end of the operation, all administrations of anesthetics were stopped, and those who underwent surgery were transported to the postanesthesia care unit with an endotracheal tube or laryngeal mask after being given 50 mg of flurbiprofen axetil. Neostigmine was taken regularly to counteract muscular relaxation. The laryngeal mask or endotracheal tube was removed once the criteria for extubation were satisfied. When the steward score was >4 points, the patients returned to the ward. An analgesic agent is deemed inadequate if the patient’s resting-state visual analogue scale (VAS) score in the surgical ward is higher three points or if the patient asks for additional analgesics. Dezocine was administered as a rescue analgesic, and the pain score was controlled at ≤3 points. Outcomes The rate of POD in both groups 5 days following surgery was the primary endpoint. The CAM was utilized in the present study to determine the presence of delirium. Five days following the procedure, the participants were evaluated twice a day using the CAM, once in the morning and once in the afternoon, with a minimum 6-hour gap between assessments. When the CAM test was positive, the type and degree of delirium were evaluated using the Delirium Rating Scale-Revised-98 (DRS-R-98). The secondary outcomes were as follows: (1) the duration and type of POD; (2) the severity of POD; (3) 10- and 20-minute coma recovery scale-revised (CRS-R) scores after extubation; (4) VAS score at 0–5 days after surgery; (5) duration of hospital stay (from the day of surgery to discharge); (6) telephone interview for cognitive status-modified (TICS-m) score at 1 month after surgery; and (7) the kinds and rates of AEs to demonstrate the safety of MB. The sample size was calculated by applying the following method: n i = 2 Z 1 − α / 2 + Z 1 − β E S 2 ES is the effect size, defined as follows: E S = p 1 − p 2 p 1 − p where | p 1– p 2| is the absolute value of the difference in proportions between two of the groups expected under the alternative hypothesis and p is the overall proportion based on pooling the data from the two comparison groups. Therefore, we needed 98 patients per group, assuming a power of 90% and an alpha error of 0.05. Based on an estimated 10% loss to follow-up rate, a total sample size of 218 was determined. Categorical data are summarized as frequencies and percentages and were compared between study groups using the chi-squared test or Fisher’s exact test, as appropriate. Continuous data are summarized as median and interquartile range (IQR) or mean and standard deviation depending on the variable distribution. Normality was evaluated using the Shapiro‒Wilk test. Independent sample t -tests were used to analyze regularly distributed data, and Mann‒Whitney U tests were used to analyze nonnormally distributed data. The generalized estimated equation was employed to examine nonnormally distributed data that were gathered at various times. Using Kaplan‒Meier survival analysis, the cumulative incidence of POD was examined, and the intergroup variations in incidence were compared using the log-rank test. In addition, logistic regression was performed to determine the impact of the intervention on the incidence of POD after adjustment for risk factors, and the results are reported as odds ratios (ORs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). All the statistical analyses were performed using SPSS 25.0. For each hypothesis, a two-sided P value < 0.05 was considered to indicate statistical significance. In-hospitalization AEs Pulse oximetry monitoring and intraoperative vital signs were unaffected by MB infusion. Notably, throughout the intraoperative period, no patient in the MB group had clinically significant hemolytic anemia or MB allergy. It was expected that individuals in the MB group would have blue‒green urine 3–5 days after surgery because MB is primarily eliminated by the kidneys. According to our findings, patients’ serum creatinine and postoperative liver enzyme levels were not considerably improved by MB infusion. The MB group had a substantially higher rate of postoperative fever (axillary temperature greater than 37.3°C) (16.5%) than did the control group (7.4%, P = 0.039; Supplementary Digital Content, Table A2, Available at; http://links.lww.com/JS9/E704 ). However, there was no statistically significant difference between the two groups in terms of the incidence of other adverse reactions. Nevertheless, the patients’ fever quickly resolved within 1–2 days, and there were no overt indications of a local or systemic infection. Owing to disagreements regarding the efficacy of most therapies for POD in clinical trials [ – ] , our research offers a potentially useful strategy for preventing POD. Inspired by the recent use of MB and its derivatives in the treatment of Alzheimer’s disease [ , ] , MB was used off-label in this investigation to prevent POD. It has also been shown that surgery and anesthesia disrupt mitochondrial fusion/fission dynamics, leading to mitochondrial dysfunction, including excessive oxidative stress and energy deficiency, ultimately leading to the development of POD [ ] . It has also been shown that surgery and anesthesia disrupt mitochondrial fusion/fission dynamics, leading to mitochondrial dysfunction, including excessive oxidative stress and energy deficiency, ultimately leading to the development of POD [ ] . Thus, interventions to protect mitochondria may be beneficial, and the beneficial neuroprotective effect of MB on mitochondria was detected in previous animal experiments [ ] , which provided the basis for our study. POD is characterized by a rapid onset and a fluctuating course. The symptoms typically manifest in episodes and start 24–72 hours following surgery [ ] . Here, we assessed the incidence of delirium in all patients for 5 consecutive days. The frequency of POD among these patients was 14.3%, comparable to earlier findings [ ] , with 8.3% of patients in the MB group and 20.4% of patients in the control group. Moreover, we observed that the majority of POD cases were hypoactive delirium (58.1%), a subtype of delirium characterized by symptoms of lethargy, stillness, immobility, and cognitive dissociation that is frequently disregarded in clinical settings. The outcomes of this research are in line with prior findings [ ] . The clinically “silent” hypoactive type may be more fatal than the hyperactive type [ ] , but the severity of delirium in the present study was milder. One month following surgery, the short half-life of MB may account for the lack of a statistically significant difference in TICS-m scores between the two groups. More research is still needed to explore the effects of varying MB delivery times and doses on POD development and delayed neurocognitive recovery. MB acts directly on the central nervous system, and its effect on the maintenance of and recovery from general anesthesia has been less studied. Previous research has indicated that administering a 5 mg/kg MB intravenous infusion 1 hour before surgery can decrease the intraoperative propofol maintenance dose and prolong recovery [ ] . According to the outcomes of the present study, there was no delay in postoperative anesthesia recovery in the two groups; however, the recovery time in the MB group was marginally longer than that in the control group. Nonetheless, there was no statistically significant difference in the intraoperative maintenance dose of propofol between the two groups. This may be due to differences in the anesthesia management protocols used during the operation. First, intraoperative propofol infusion did not implement target-controlled infusion during the anesthesia maintenance period. Second, we used to increase the concentration of inhaled anesthetics to adjust for increases in patients’ heart rates and blood pressure without recording the dosage of inhaled anesthetics. Consequently, more research is still required to fully understand the mechanism and connection between MB and anesthetics. The CRS-R reflects the patient’s state of consciousness through six behavioral aspects: visual, auditory, motor, verbal, communication, and arousal. It can be used for ongoing evaluation and is simple to use, so the CRS-R scale was used in this study to evaluate the consciousness of patients during recovery from general anesthesia. The results indicated that there was no statistically significant difference in CRS-R scores between 10 and 20 minutes after extubation, suggesting that MB could temporarily prolong patient recovery but did not affect the recovery of consciousness during the recovery period. Perioperative hepatic and renal function in elderly patients is a safety concern. However, this study did not find that MB had an impact on the functionality of these essential organs. There was no significant difference in the incidence of abnormal liver function or renal function between the two groups. In our study, postoperative fever was more common in the MB group, which rapidly resolved within 1 day or 2 days, and no serious local or systemic infection was found, although the etiology was unknown. The other side effects were not significantly different between the two groups. The gradual dosing (given within 60 minutes) and single dose of MB (2 mg/kg) may be the reason why the monitoring equipment was not tampered with during the surgery. This study has several limitations. First, there may be observational bias, as blue urine cannot cause blindness in patients. In addition, this inadvertent observation may affect the patient’s concentration so that they no longer meet the criteria for “inattention,” a crucial factor in the diagnosis of delirium. In future studies, a group of low doses of MB, such as 0.2 mg/kg, could also turn the urine color blue as a control. Finally, objective indicators, such as biomarkers, were not detected to explore the effects of MB on patients. Given that MB has antineuroinflammatory and protective effects on mitochondria, combining MB with biomarkers may help clarify the mitochondrial mechanism of delirium, although the exact cause of this condition is still unknown. In conclusion, our research revealed that intraoperative intravenous infusion of 2 mg/kg of MB decreased the incidence of POD in older patients who underwent THA or TKA during the hospital stay but did not significantly increase the incidence or extent of adverse reactions, showing that MB may be a safe and clinically useful medication for preventing POD. Clinical studies with more volunteers are required to confirm this novel treatment.

Introduction The World Health Organization (WHO) estimates that the proportion of people over 60 years old will have doubled by 2050. This age group will account for more than two billion people by 2050, compared to 900 million in 2015 ( ). By general comparison, the Swiss population of older adults has a good general health status ( ). However, age-related biological changes including but not limited to sarcopenia, reduced abilities in walking, balance and coordination, sight disorders, cognitive decline and comorbidities are risk factors associated with a sharp increase in falls prevalence. For example, in Switzerland, prevalence over the population increased from 21% in 2002 to 26% in 2017 ( ). Polypharmacy and home hazards may also enhance this risk ( ; ; ). Worldwide, 28% to 35% of people over 64 years and 32% to 42% of those over 70 suffer of a fall each year. This phenomenon raises with age and level of frailty ( ). Fatal but also non-fatal injuries amongst older adults over 65 years old are mainly attributable to falls ( ). Of the 36 million falls in older adults in the United States of America, 20% will have severe consequences such as fractures or head injuries ( ). Those can strongly impact people’s quality of life, health and lifestyle ( ). Indeed, 21% to 85% of victims of a fall will experience physical, functional, psychological and social changes ( ). Therefore, a fear of falling can arise, with negative consequences on physical and functional well-being ( ), and a heightened risk of future falls ( ; ). The falls consequences remain various and can be far-reaching: chronic pain, loss of mobility and autonomy, anxiety, long-term hospitalisations or placements in healthcare centres ( ; ). This can lead to significant direct financial costs. For example, in Switzerland, hospitalisation for a hip fracture costs CHF 15,000 ( ), and a year spent in an institution around CHF 100,000 per person ( ; ). In addition, indirect costs, including losses due to premature death, morbidity or disability, unpaid activities, care services, but also intangible costs related to pain and loss of quality of life, are also attributable to falls ( ). Globally, the socio-economic costs (material and immaterial) related to falls amounted to CHF 14.7 billion in 2017 in Switzerland ( ). Guidelines ( ; ; ; ; ), clinical guidance statements ( ), and systematic reviews ( ; ; ; ), have emphasised the effectiveness of multifactorial assessments for determining the risk of falling and for informing the implementation of personalised fall prevention strategies ( ). It is recommended that older adults over 65 years old should regularly (at least once per year) be assessed for fall risk, e.g. by asking about their fall histories, frequencies, contexts and characteristics ( ). As movement specialists, physiotherapists constitute a primary point of intervention in preventing falls ( ). They can, for example, inform physicians and home care agencies regarding fall risk factors ( ). Effective fall prevention interventions involve three main steps. First, the screening enables detection of increased fall risk. For example, inquiring regularly about falls history can help to identify individuals at higher risk of future falls. Second, intrinsic and extrinsic factors are investigated through additional assessments such as medication review, mobility level, posture, blood pressure, vision, gait and balance, lower extremity joint function, neurologic and cognitive function, muscular strength, proprioception, reflexes, and/or environmental assessment. Finally, appropriate interventions aim to reduce the rate of falls and the severity of injury. Multidimensional individualised exercise programs are considered a reliable method of preventing falls in older persons ( ; ; ). However, little is known about the current practices of physiotherapists concerning fall prevention. To our knowledge, there are no published data on the implementation of fall risk assessment guidelines by physiotherapists in Switzerland. To ensure our profession provides guideline-recommended care for older adults, it is necessary to review current clinical practices in screening fall risk in patients over 65 years old. Therefore, this online survey sought to evaluate to what extent physiotherapists carry out fall risk assessments as the first step towards a fall prevention intervention in the population of community-dwelling older adults in Switzerland. The aim was to determine whether current practices are in line with current recommendations. After identifying barriers and facilitators to fall risk assessment, recommendations on appropriate clinical resources and targeted training will be proposed. Methods Study design A cross-sectional survey of physiotherapists currently practising in Switzerland was undertaken between the 21st of November and the 31st of December 2020. Participants Registered physiotherapists working in Switzerland and providing care to patients over the age of 65 in their daily practice were eligible to participate. Two mandatory screening questions were used to confirm eligibility: i) Are you currently (or in the last 12 months) working as a physiotherapist in Switzerland? ii) Are you managing patients over 65, regardless of their initial pathology? Recruitment strategy In the absence of a federal register comprising all currently practising physiotherapists in Switzerland, a comprehensive recruitment strategy was developed by the research team. It was designed to optimise the results generalisability and sample representativeness. Therefore, a range of organisations was asked to assist with study recruitment by sending the questionnaire to their members, which maintained confidentiality. First, all Swiss cantonal physiotherapy associations were invited to participate. Sending confirmations were received from Bern, Valais, Basel, Neuchâtel, and Aargau organisations. Additionally, the Swiss Association of Independent Physiotherapists (ASPI-SVFP) and the Swiss Association of Sports Physiotherapy (Sportfisio) also agreed to send the study questionnaire to their members. To broaden the sampling frame, Master’s students in physiotherapy at the Bern University of Applied Sciences (BFH) and the Zürich University of Applied Sciences (ZHAW), as well as ALUMNI physiotherapists from the HES-SO Valais-Wallis, were invited to participate. Moreover, lists of physiotherapy practices (n=2000) for each of the 26 Swiss cantons were created manually with online research on local.ch . Finally, the questionnaire was sent to all physiotherapists working on the Swiss CHEF Trial project. This ongoing national randomized controlled trial compares three home-based exercises programs aiming at preventing falls in older people of Switzerland ( ). Non-monetary incentives To maximise responses, all the participants who took part in the survey had the opportunity to participate in a prize draw ( ; ; ). Three prizes were offered, consisting of an overnight hotel stay. To ensure the anonymity of the survey responses, a separate webpage was used to collect and store the email addresses. There was no link between survey responses and email addresses stored for the prize draw. Survey development A draft questionnaire was developed using an iterative process with the research team, which included six physiotherapists with several years of experience in fall prevention and geriatrics. Permission to use clinical practice questionnaires developed for similar studies was obtained from two authors ( ; ). Ackerman et al. targeted fall prevention by older people with osteoarthritis and Gaboreau et al. focussed their study on general practitioners’ (GPs) routines linked to this topic. Their questionnaires were partially adapted to align with the research question and Swiss healthcare context. To maximise study quality and research rigour, the Checklist for Reporting Results of Internet E-Surveys (CHERRIES, see extended data “CHERRIES Checklist” ( )) ( ), results of different guidelines, systematic reviews and studies ( ; ; ; ; ) as well as websites ( ; ; ) were followed. See extended data “Designing Tools” for brief descriptions of each of the tools mentioned above ( ). The semi-structured online questionnaire consisted of 52 short questions with several branching logics (adaptive questioning). This process allowed some questions to be displayed conditionally based on the answers to prior items, intentionally reducing the responder burden. The survey included a mix of open-ended questions and multiple response options covering first participants characteristics. As no identifying information was collected, the anonymity of the participants was preserved. Workplace, assessed only with the first two postal code numbers, was used to observe the presence of falls prevention programmes by geographical area. Perceived ability to assess and manage older patients was evaluated on two purposed-designed Likert scales ranging from 0 “none” to 100 “excellent”. The responsibility of nine health care professions in fall risk assessment was also questioned on Likert scales ranging from 0 “not at all concerned” to 10 “very concerned”. The way physiotherapists screen for fall risk included questions about the situations leading to testing the patient, the tests used, and the interventions undertaken. Risk factors and the way they are measured were also evaluated. One question specifically targeted the reasons why some therapists never assess fall risk to understand barriers to fall risk assessment. How physiotherapists quantified the risk of falling, reassessed patients and the elements needed to facilitate a more systematic risk assessment were asked at the end of the questionnaire. Three hypothetical patient cases (vignettes) from the musculoskeletal, respiratory, and neurological fields were also presented to respondents and their management related to fall risk assessment evaluated. The different steps of survey validation were conducted with the help of 21 physiotherapists who were experienced in the treatment of older adults and measurement properties. Questionnaire feasibility was assessed, as well as content and face validity and comprehensibility. Dillman developed a four-step methodological pre-testing process adapted and applied for this study to assess validity according to Artino et al. recommendations ( ; ). Assessment of reliability Reliability and validity are essential scores to consider when elaborating a questionnaire ( ). Validity assessment was undertaken following the pre-test process of Dillman ( ), and modifications were undertaken if necessary. To meet the 31st of December 2020 deadline for completion of data collection, this step was first not evaluated. One reminder was sent to all participants three weeks after the initial mailing (i.e. 08.12.2020) to increase response rates ( ; ; ). Data collection was completed by the 31st of December 2020. All details regarding survey distribution and follow-up are described in extended data “Survey Send Out” ( ). The cover letter gave an overview of the study's main objectives and efforts to preserve participant confidentiality and anonymity (see extended data “Cover Letter” ( )). It was specified that by submitting the two eligibility assessment questions, informed consent was implied. Eligible participants were led to the survey, and those considered ineligible were informed that they could not take part. Participation could involve any electronic device, and the estimated duration did not exceed 25 minutes. At no time were an IP tracking or cookies used. No other techniques to analyse the log file for the identification of multiple entries were used. The link to the online survey was posted on the project website but no other advertisement was done. Ethical approval An approval of Swiss Ethics was obtained via the “Clarification of responsibility” form on the portal of the Business Administration System for Ethics Committees (BASEC) in May 2020. As the survey was anonymous and no health-related data were asked, this study did not fall under the Swiss Human Research Act (CER-VD Req-2020-00515). Data analysis Data were analysed with R, version 4.0.5 ( ), RStudio, version 1.4.1106 ( ) and Stata (Version 17, StataCorp, College Station, Texas) ( ). Handling of variable’s grouping When evaluating how physiotherapists assess the fall risk of their patients, of the 938 participants, only 8 (0,1%) reported that they never assess the fall risk. Therefore, it was decided not to use this item to test the hypotheses. Instead, a binary variable “use standardised assessment” was created from the four response options: i) By a subjective evaluation (observation of the patient, discussion…), ii) By a standardised evaluation (scale, functional tests, questionnaires, timed tests…) iii) By instrumental assessment (inertial sensors, force platforms, EMG…) iv) I do not perform an assessment. We dichotomised them as follows: “use standardised assessment”: yes = ii) & iii), no = i) & iv). We categorised the year of completion of the highest education level as follows: i) “Before 1990”: < 1990, ii) “1990 to 1999”: > 1990 & < 2000, iii) “2000 to 2009”: > 2000 & < 2010, iii) “2010 or later”: > 2010. A binary variable “Clinic or Private Practice” was created from the different work settings: i) Hospital, ii) Rehabilitation clinic, iii) Private practice as employee, iv) Private practice as self-employed person, v) Retirement home, vi) Home-based physiotherapist, vi) Other(s). We dichotomised them as follows: “Institution” = i) & ii) & v), “Private practice” = iii) & iv) & v) & vi). Vignettes of patients with musculoskeletal, neurological, or respiratory problems were presented: i) A 65-year-old man consults for rheumatological problems (e.g., Osteoarthritis). His physiotherapy referral mentions "anti-inflammatory analgesia, improvement of joint and muscle function". What do you do? ii) A 72-year-old woman consults because of neurological problems (e.g., Parkinson's disease). Her physiotherapy referral mentions "improvement of joint and muscle function, proprioception/coordination". What do you do? iii) A 68-year-old man consults because of respiratory disease (e.g., Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease). His physiotherapy referral mentions "improvement of cardiopulmonary function". What do you do? Statistics The distributions of the continuous variables were analysed visually, and median, interquartile range, minimal and maximal values were reported. Categorical variables were summarised with absolute and relative frequencies. 95% confidence intervals were reported to document the statistical precision of the estimates. The significance level was set at p<0.05 for all tests. Differences between participants with more than 10% missing values and those with fewer missing values were compared with non-parametric tests for continuous variables and with Chi-squared tests for frequency tables. Cohen’s d effect size was calculated for continuous variables. An effect size of 0.2 was considered a slight difference, 0.5 a moderate difference and 0.8 a significant difference. Cramer’s V effect sizes were calculated for categorical variables, where 0.1 was considered small, 0.3 moderate and 0.5 large. The hypotheses were tested using multivariable logistic regression for binary dependent variables and Chi-squared tests for categorical dependent variables. The logistical and linear regressions were adjusted for a set of potential confounders. Variables for the multivariable models were selected using Directed Acyclic Graphs (DAGs) according to theoretical considerations ( ). Nonparametric Cochran-Armitage statistics was used to test trend (i.e., hypothesis 2, increasing proportion of physiotherapists assessing with increasing education level). Contrast after an ANOVA was used to test whether the responsibility for screening was higher for physiotherapists as for other professions (hypothesis 5). An additional exploratory analysis was performed. i.e., it has been clearly stated that no a priori hypothesis was formulated and that this result needed to be interpreted with caution. The textual content of the semi-open questions (n=13) was analysed through a content analysis using an inductive approach ( ; ). This analysis approach was the most feasible due to the extensive data and the human resources available. Each free text response (meaning unit) was closely reviewed and summarised into main concepts (condensed meaning units). Those were then grouped into emerging themes making clinical or theoretical sense. To illustrate them, some participants' responses are provided verbatim in their original language. Finally, because there was some evidence of differences regarding fall risk activities and admission patterns to nursing home according to Swiss cantons ( ), it was decided to present the descriptive results stratified per language. Response ratio According to the Swiss Federal Statistical Office (FSO), it was impossible to know the official number of physiotherapists currently practising in Switzerland. Because third parties sent invitation emails, we do not know the number of emails delivered. Therefore, the response ratio could not be calculated. Sample size considerations The members of the national physiotherapy association, Physioswiss (n=10’652 in December 2019), and the Swiss Association of Independent Physiotherapists, ASPI-SVFP (n=500 in December 2019) were added to estimate the Swiss population of working physiotherapists, acknowledging that not all physiotherapists are members of one of these associations or that a potential overlap might occur. With an estimated precision of 5% (i.e. 95% confidence interval span of 10%) and an estimated population of 11'155 individuals, complete answers of 371 therapists were required ( The Survey System ). This calculation required the assumption of random sampling, i.e., that our sample is representative of all physiotherapists working in Switzerland. However, we were not able to test this assumption. Results Reliability The median ICC (for the ordinal and continuous variables) was 0.86, with only one item below 0.7. The median Kappa value for the dichotomous items was 0.65, with 15% of items with Kappa values below 0.41. The items with lower than moderate Kappa values (i.e. <0.41) were items with many multiple choice response options (e.g. the type of falls screening tool used, the advice given regarding falls risk the type of balance assessments used). Furthermore, the responses for the question about which professionals are responsible for the screening of falls risk, the results for the nurses and occupational therapist had too low Kappa values. Survey responses A total of 981 individuals completed the two screening questions to assess their eligibility. Among them, 938 (95.6%) were eligible to participate. 715 (76.2%) physiotherapists (PTs) responded to at least 90% of the questions, 714 (76.1%) to the last question and 224 (23.9%) excited the survey prematurely, only providing partial data. All questionnaire data, even partially completed, were imported, analysed, and the attrition ratio (number of missing values per item) taken into consideration. The participants flow chart is presented in . Atypical timestamps The median participation time was 17 minutes (IQR 11 to 27), and no participant data were excluded because of atypical time required to complete the questionnaire. Completion ratio and missing values The completion ratio for this study was 76.1%. The percentage of missing responses per items ranged from 0 to 24% (see extended data “Missing Values” ( )). The sensitivity analyses with the comparison of those with more than 10% missing responses to those with fewer missing responses showed several differences between both groups. Participants with more missing responses were three years older (Cohen’s d of 0.24, p<0.05) and less frequently had an education with a bachelor’s degree or higher (Cramer’s V effect size 0.13, p<0.05). Moreover, they also had 10% more participants who received their diploma before 1990 (p<0.05), 12% more who worked in private practice as employees (Cramer’s V effect size 0.13, p<0.05), and 7% less who worked in hospitals (Cramer’s V effect size 0.09, p<0.05). Furthermore, those with more missing values reported less confidence in the assessment of the fall risk (Cohen’s d 0.25, p<0.05) and less confidence in the management of people with an increased fall risk (Cohen’s d 0.19, p<0.05), compared to those with less missing values. Because of these systematic differences, it was decided not to exclude those with more than 10% missing as it would induce a sampling bias. Characteristics of physiotherapists assessing their patients First, the main characteristics related to the practice of fall risk assessment were investigated. Hypothesis 1a (H1a): Standardised tests or instruments are reported to be used by 580 (62%) PTs to evaluate fall risk and subjective assessment was used by 729 (77.7%) PTs (see ). When participants were split into mutually exclusive categories regarding their risk assessment approach, it was observed that 49% performed a combination of subjective and standardised fall risk evaluation while 25% evaluated the risk only with a subjective assessment. Less than 5% used an instrumented evaluation (see ). The odds of using a standardised assessment were 1.93 times higher for participants working in a clinic or hospital setting (institutional context) compared to those working in private practice (adjusted OR 1.93, 95% CI 1.37 to 2.7). H1b: 96 (36%) PTs working in an institutional setting and 129 (21%) of those working in private practice used a standardised instrument for 50% to 94% of their older patients. Furthermore, only 38 (14%) of those working in a clinic or hospital setting and 25 (4%) in private practice used it systematically, i.e., in at least 95% of their patients (χ 2 70.8662, df 3, p <0.001). H7: The two most frequently factors leading PTs to assess their patients were the history of falls (n=469, 87.7%) and the evocation of a fear of falling (n=469, 87.7%). H9: PTs who regularly performed fall risk assessment used a specific tool more often than those who evaluated it less often. Significant between-group differences were not always observed, but for those with p<0.05, the physiotherapist reporting evaluating fall risk “always” chose these tests more often compared to the physiotherapist assessing less often. There was one exception, the Timed-Up and Go (TUG), where therapists reporting assessing fall risk "often" (n=158, 70.2%) chose it more frequently than those who assess "always" (n=44, 69.8%). Exploratory analyses A post-hoc hypothesis concerning the influence of the initial pathology on the assessment of the risk of falls was made during the statistical analysis. This result should be treated with caution. To address the hypothesis that the assessment rate could be different in patients with musculoskeletal, neurological or respiratory pathologies, three hypothetical patient vignettes were used. In patients with musculoskeletal problems, 91% of the PTs assessed fall risk factors (99% of PTs in patients with neurological, and 74% in patients with respiratory pathologies). For the use of a standardised fall risk tool, only 11.3% of the PTs would have assessed patients with musculoskeletal problems, 48.4% of the PTs patients with neurological and 10% PTs patients with a respiratory disease). Thus, our post-hoc hypothesis that patients with neurological conditions are more frequently assessed for fall risk than those with other pathologies was confirmed. Content analysis Open-ended questions (n=13) allowed participants to express themselves freely on different aspects related to fall risk assessment. The ideas underlying some of the themes are developed below, supported by verbatim quotes in their original language. All themes extracted from the analysis of these open-ended questions are presented in extended data “Extracted Themes” ( ). Other situations leading to fall risk assessment Other situations than those mentioned in the questionnaire may lead PTs to assess their patients' risk of falling. If this is not done during the initial assessment, the therapist might observe that the patient has balance problems when moving, exercising, or using walking aids. This may lead to a more detailed risk assessment. Return home after hospitalisation may also prompt PTs to assess the risk of falls of their patients. Other standardised assessments used Other assessments closely or remotely related to the risk of falls used by the PTs interviewed were: i) Functional Independence Measure (FIM), ii) Hierarchical Assessment of Balance and Mobility (HABAM), iii) Limit of stability test (LOS), iv) Modified Romberg Test (mRomberg), v) Multiple Sclerosis Questionnaire for Physiotherapists (MSQPT), vi) Romberg Test, and vii) The de Morton Mobility Index (DEMMI). Static balance assessment Static balance was assessed through various tests such as the One-Legged stance Test (OLST) or Single Leg Stance (SLS), or the 4-Stage Balance Scale Test. Some tests used such as the Berg Balance Scale (BBS) or the Balance Evaluation Systems Test (BESTest) examine both static and dynamic balance. PTs also mentioned testing balance on an unstable surface or with eyes closed without specifying whether this was done in a standardised way or not. Finally, the use of devices that also assess dynamic balance, such as the Huber 360 Evolution ® or the Galileo ® , was also stated. Participants who did not assess static balance gave reasons such as lack of knowledge, of specific tests, or of time during the initial assessment. For others, testing did not contribute to diagnosis and management and was therefore not considered necessary. A focus was placed on the reason for the initial consultation, thus favouring treatment over assessment. Dynamic balance assessment Dynamic balance was assessed using walking tests (6 Minutes or 10 Meter Walk Tests), mixed assessments such as the Tinetti Balance Assessment Tool (Tinetti/POMA) or the Short Physical Performance Battery (SPPB), and assessments whose standardisation remains uncertain such as walking on a line, backwards, or sideways for example. Devices such as the GaitUp System ® or the Dividat Senso ® were also mentioned. The reasons for not assessing dynamic balance were similar to those reported for static balance. However, the lack of space to carry out the assessment was also reported.
